newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebel attack is bid to save dying MRTA group.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebel attack is bid to save dying MRTA group.

text.p: The siege of the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima by the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) is a last ditch attempt to relaunch a group as most of its members languish in prison, analysts said on Friday.
"They were decimated. They are playing their final card in a bid to resuscitate their movement," said Peruvian sociologist Raul Gonzalez. "It is an all or nothing act."
The MRTA currently has no more than 80 active members, down from around 800 in the late 1980s, and about 450 of their members were behind bars, Peruvian guerrilla expert Carlos Tapia said.

Violence in Peru provoked by the MRTA and the much larger and previously better-known Maoist Shining Path peaked during the late 1980s and early 1990s but had died down considerably since the captures of key guerrilla leaders in 1992.

The MRTA gained support in its early days in the mid-1980s as a Robin Hood-style movement that robbed the rich to give to the poor, hijacking trucks and distributing the goods to peasants. But it eventually lost public sympathy after turning increasingly to kidnapping, bombing and drug activities.
Unlike the Shining Path, the MRTA had never posed a serious threat to national security, Tapia said.

"I do not see the MRTA killing anybody (at the residence). Their operation has not been one of systematic violence. They are an operation in decline but have demonstrated their capacity to put these spectacular operations together," said David Scott Palmer, an author on Peruvian guerrillas based in Boston.

The MRTA was reponsible for the deaths of no more than 200 Peruvian soldiers and police out of an estimated total of 30,000 lives lost in the country's 16-year guerrilla conflicts, according to Tapia.
It never before conducted a notable attack in the capital but the group plotted a similar, high-profile assault on Congress last year that was thwarted by anti-terrorist police.

While Gonzalez believed the attack was a sincere attempt to swell its dwindling ranks by gaining the release of its jailed comrades, Tapia and Palmer said the MRTA was hoping to lay down its arms and become a strictly political movement.
"They have a lot of demands but in practice they want to be incorporated within the law in politics," Tapia said.
The embassy siege put the group in the international spotlight and gave them the opportunity "to play up their Robin Hood image and at the right moment become a political movement," Palmer said.
The siege was a way of forcing the government to consider this possibility in the face of President Alberto Fujimori's consistent, hardline stance not to negotiate with guerrillas, Tapia said.
Peruvians were surprised at the boldness of the MRTA's assault on Tuesday, but not at the careful planning involved.
"They have always used their brains. They are intelligent, much more intelligent than the Shining Path, who just kill everybody and damage everything," Lima taxi driver Ricardo Mendes said.

The group's most famous alleged member is an American woman, Lori Berenson, 27, who is serving a life sentence at the 13,000 feet- (4,000 metre-) high Yanamayo maximum security prison in Puno in southern Peru.

Captured following the breakup of the unit plotting the congressional takeover, Berenson was accused of being a leader of the MRTA, renting a house in Lima as a front for the guerrillas, transporting arms, helping to prepare psychologically rebel fighters, and gathering intelligence by posing as a journalist for U.S.-based magazines.

Since her conviction, there has been a growing campaign in the United States -- actively supported by former President Jimmy Carter -- to annul the decison of the military courts, where anonymous judges usually wear hoods and do not allow cross-examination.
At its height of power in the late 1980s, the MRTA counted on 800 active members and was a powerful influence in the rebel stronghold in the central jungle region of the Huallaga valley.

But increasingly strong links with Peru's illegal drugs trade based in the valley region "split up the group" and the 1992 capture of its leader Victor Polay left the MRTA as a largely spent force, according to Tapia.
